newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish premier seen set to survive China row.
newsitem.headline: Swedish premier seen set to survive China row.

text.p: Opposition parties on Wednesday tabled a no-confidence motion against Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson over remarks which they said implied praise for China's political stability.
Persson, who made an official visit to China this month, defended his comments in a special debate and looked certain to survive if and when the motion came to a no-confidence vote in parliament.
The Conservative, Liberal and Christian Democratic parties said they tabled the motion on the grounds that Persson had damaged Swedish interests.
He had told Swedish businessmen in Beijing: "To me, it's striking what political stability means for economic development when you look at the Chinese example."

Defending his comments in a special parliamentary debate on Wednesday, Social Democratic leader Persson said the whole affair had been exaggerated, adding: "I never placed any value judgement on the phrase 'political stability'."

Conservative parliamentary group leader Lars Tobisson said he was surprised Persson had repeated without apology his comment that "if there is infringement of human rights, of course one would protest".
"There is no if about it," Tobisson said. "Trampling on human rights doesn't just happen here and there in China. Oppression is in the nature of a communist disctatorship."
Persson described criticism of his remarks as "grotesque", and assured parliament that he had raised human rights questions in his talks with premier Jiang Zemin and other Chinese leaders.
Earlier on Wednesday Persson was also called to explain his remarks at Sweden's foreign policy advisory council, an all-party forum chaired by the king, Carl XVI Gustav.

The burly politician, who took over as leader of Sweden's ruling party when Ingvar Carlsson stepped down in March, may face a no-confidence motion in parliament on Friday, Swedish political commentators said.
But Persson was certain to survive the vote after the Leftist party, which has enabled his minority Social Democrats to govern, said it would back him.
Another party, the Greens, said they would abstain from the vote, while the Centre Party had not decided but was believed unlikely to vote against Persson.

Liberal party member Lars Leijonborg told Reuters: "It looks unlikely that there will be a majority (for no-confidence). But even a majority of no-confidence votes and abstentions would be a severe check on the government."
